analysis.one_liner: Bars police from running facial recognition on body-worn camera footage.
analysis.headline: The bill to stop police facial recognition scans of body-worn camera video never got a hearing or a vote and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would stop federal, state, and local police from using facial recognition or other biometric identification on footage from officers' body-worn cameras. It would enforce the ban by cutting 5 percent of certain federal public-safety grants from governments that break the rule, with the money shifted to governments that follow it. The bill's stated reasons: facial recognition misidentifies women, young people, and people of color; it turns accountability cameras into tracking tools; and it chills free speech and cooperation with police in heavily policed neighborhoods.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of heavily policed communities, especially people of color who are misidentified by facial recognition at higher rates, anyone who protests or speaks in public without wanting to be tracked, and crime victims who avoid police contact. People who use body-worn cameras as intended—as accountability tools rather than surveillance dragnets—also benefit.

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits federal law enforcement agencies, states, local governments, and high-risk urban areas from running facial recognition or other biometric surveillance on any image captured by a police body-worn camera, and bars agencies from getting around the ban by asking a third party to run the scan for them [S2] [S3].

It enforces the ban by cutting 5 percent of federal justice and homeland-security grants (Byrne Grants, the Urban Area Security Initiative, and State Homeland Security Grants) from governments that violate it, and shifting that money to governments that comply [S2] [S3].

The bill's findings state that facial recognition misidentifies women, young people, and people of color at elevated rates, would create massive databases about law-abiding Americans, would chill free speech in public places, and would discourage people in highly policed communities from cooperating with police [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Police departments that want to scan body-camera footage through facial recognition databases would lose access to that practice. Facial recognition vendors would lose a growing customer base. If a government kept using the technology anyway, its residents would effectively pay, through a 5 percent cut to federal public-safety grant money.
analysis.who_pays_short: Facial recognition vendors and police agencies

drawbacks.text: The enforcement tool withholds federal grant money, so the cost of a violation falls partly on the residents of the violating jurisdiction—less grant funding for their public-safety programs—rather than only on the officials who broke the rule [S3].
The ban covers only images acquired by body-worn cameras, leaving facial recognition on other police imagery—station cameras, dashcams, third-party databases—unaddressed [S2] [S3].

Police supporters argue the technology can help identify suspects in serious crimes, and the bill forecloses that use on body-camera footage; a supporter would have to concede some investigations become harder [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill protects people from a form of surveillance that its own findings say misidentifies women, young people, and people of color at elevated rates, and it closes the loophole where police ask an outside company to run the scan. The main costs are narrow: the grant-penalty mechanism can cut funding from a violator's own residents, and the ban leaves big facial-recognition gaps on non-body-camera imagery. A reasonable bill with a limited reach.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in June 2020, sent to the Judiciary and Homeland Security committees, referred to a homeland security subcommittee in August, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Don Beyer introduced the bill on June 18, 2020, with 7 original cosponsors, amid the national debate over policing after George Floyd's murder [S1] [S3].
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee and the Homeland Security Committee on the day of introduction; dual referrals mean both committees would need to act for the bill to advance [S5].
On August 1, 2020, it was referred to the Homeland Security Subcommittee on Emergency Preparedness, Response, and Recovery, and no further action was taken [S5].
No hearings, markups, or votes are recorded in the bill's action history; the bill expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Police agencies and facial-recognition vendors kept an unrestricted ability to scan body-worn camera footage; no community gained protections.

for.name: Rep. Don Beyer
for.role: Sponsor, House Democratic chief deputy whip-elect; representor of a Northern Virginia district
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban facial recognition scans of body-worn camera footage and sought cosponsors.

for.name: 8 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; none of the 197 House Republicans cosponsored.

sides.party_line_note: No opposing action is recorded because the bill never advanced to a vote; all sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republican cosponsored [S4].

industries.industry: Facial recognition and biometric surveillance vendors
industries.note: The bill would cut off a growing market: police scanning body-worn camera footage against face databases, directly or through third parties. Its product's documented misidentification of women, young people, and people of color is the civil-rights problem the bill targets [S3].

The bill removes one investigative tool—identifying people from body-camera footage—and attaches a 5 percent federal grant penalty for using it, though it leaves facial recognition on other police imagery untouched [S2] [S3].
